title: Embeddings

techniques.name: Semantic Embeddings
techniques.q: Which texts mean the same thing?
techniques.what: An embedding model maps text to a dense vector, typically a few hundred to a few thousand numbers, so that texts with similar meaning land close together. Search becomes a nearest-neighbour lookup by cosine similarity, which matches paraphrases and synonyms that share no words at all.
use: Users describe things in their own words, not your terminology
Question answering over documentation or knowledge bases
Clustering, deduplication and recommendations
metrics: split documents into passages, ~200–800 tokens, with overlap
query and document embedded separately, compared fast
compare on MTEB, then on your own queries
steps: Chunk documents on natural boundaries such as headings and paragraphs, with a little overlap
Embed chunks with the same model you will use for queries
Store vectors with metadata: source, section, date, permissions
Measure recall@k on real questions before tuning anything else
pitfalls: Weak on exact terms: IDs, codes, rare names
Domain jargon may need a domain-tuned model
Changing models means re-embedding the whole corpus
techniques.cap: The query shares no words with “refund policy”, yet it lands in the refunds cluster.

techniques.name: Sparse Keyword Search (BM25)
techniques.q: Which documents contain these exact words?
techniques.what: BM25 is the classic ranking function behind most keyword search engines. It scores a document by how often the query terms appear (with diminishing returns), how rare those terms are across the collection, and the document’s length. It needs no training, runs fast, and excels at exact matches.
use: Queries with error codes, SKUs, product names or people’s names
Technical jargon the embedding model has never seen
As the sparse half of a hybrid search
metrics: rare terms count more than common ones
one dimension per vocabulary term, mostly zeros
SPLADE adds learned term expansion to the sparse idea
steps: Tokenize consistently: lowercase, stemming, language-aware analyzers
Index fields separately (title, body) and boost the important ones
Keep BM25 alongside vector search and fuse the results
Test on queries with codes, names and exact phrases
pitfalls: No synonyms: “car” doesn’t match “automobile”
Sensitive to tokenization and language
Keyword stuffing can game the ranking
techniques.remember: Exact words, rare terms, fast answers.
techniques.cap: IDF values are illustrative. The rare token E1045 dominates the score.

techniques.name: Multimodal Embeddings
techniques.q: Can one search cover text, images and more?
techniques.what: Multimodal models embed different kinds of content into one shared vector space, so a text query can find an image and an image can find related text. CLIP-style models learn this by aligning millions of images with their captions.
use: Product catalogues searched by description or photo
Slides, scanned pages and documents full of charts
Media libraries: photos, video frames, audio
metrics: text and images compared with the same cosine similarity
text → image, image → text, image → image
embed page screenshots to keep tables and charts (e.g. ColPali)
steps: Pick a model that covers your media types and languages
Embed images (or page renders) and text into the same index
Store a link to the original asset and any extracted text as metadata
Test cross-modal queries in both directions with real examples
pitfalls: Fine visual detail such as small text or exact counts is often lost
Larger vectors and more storage per item
Quality varies a lot by domain, e.g. medical images or engineering drawings
techniques.cap: Squares are images, the circle is the text query. It lands beside the matching photos.

techniques.name: Contrastive Embeddings
techniques.q: How do I make vectors fit my domain?
techniques.what: Contrastive learning is how most embedding models are trained, and how you fine-tune one on your own data. The model sees an anchor, a positive (a true match) and negatives, and learns to pull positives closer while pushing negatives apart. Hard negatives, which look similar but are wrong, teach the most.
use: Specialised jargon: legal, medical, internal product names
Off-the-shelf models that rank near-misses above true matches
You have real signals: clicks, tickets, Q&A pairs
metrics: question ↔ correct passage, query ↔ clicked result
other examples in the batch act as negatives
steps: Collect pairs from real signals: search clicks, support tickets, Q&A logs
Mine hard negatives with your current retriever
Fine-tune a strong base model with a contrastive loss
Compare recall@k with the base model on a held-out set
pitfalls: False negatives (actually relevant passages) confuse training
Overfitting to a small dataset hurts general queries
A fine-tuned model means re-embedding the whole corpus
techniques.remember: Pull matches in, push look-alikes out.
techniques.cap: The dashed ring is “close enough to retrieve”. Training moves the right points inside it.

techniques.name: Matryoshka, Quantised and Reduced Embeddings
techniques.q: Can the vectors be smaller without losing recall?
techniques.what: Shrink vectors to save memory, storage and search time. Matryoshka-trained models let you simply keep the first dimensions. Quantization stores each value in fewer bits. PCA projects onto the directions that matter most. Recall usually drops a little, so measure it.
use: Large corpora where the index no longer fits in memory
Latency budgets that full-size vectors can’t meet
Edge or mobile search with tight storage
metrics: keep, say, the first 256 of 1,536 dimensions
1 bit per dimension: 32× smaller; re-rank with full vectors
project onto the top principal components
2-D views for inspection, not for search
steps: Record baseline recall@k and memory at full size
Try truncation (if the model supports it) and int8 quantization first
For very large corpora, use binary quantization with a full-precision re-rank
Choose the smallest setting whose recall loss you can accept
pitfalls: Truncating a model not trained for it loses a lot of quality
Binary vectors need oversampling and re-ranking
2-D plots distort distances, so don’t draw conclusions from them alone

techniques.name: Multilingual and Code-Mixed Embeddings
techniques.q: Can one search serve Hindi, Hinglish and English?
techniques.what: A multilingual embedding model maps English, Hindi in Devanagari and Roman-script Hinglish into one vector space, so “when will my refund arrive”, “पैसा कब आएगा” and “paisa kab aayega” land near the same English article. The work is choosing a model that covers your languages, normalising scripts before embedding, deciding whether to index translated copies, and measuring recall separately for each language. It builds on dense semantic embeddings; speech and voice input are a separate technique.
use: Customers write in Hindi, other Indian languages or Hinglish, but the help content is in English
Cross-lingual search: a Hindi query should find an English circular or policy
Any product whose overall search score looks fine but whose regional users complain
metrics: e.g. BGE-M3, multilingual-e5, Cohere Embed multilingual: one space for about 100 languages
a Hindi query finds an English article with no translation step
Unicode NFC, then Roman Hindi transliterated to Devanagari
Hindi versions indexed beside English: more recall, twice the vectors
recall@5 for English, Hindi and Hinglish reported separately
Devanagari often needs more tokens per word than English
steps: Label a test set by language, including real Hinglish taken from chat logs
Compare a multilingual model with your English baseline on every language slice
Normalise Unicode and transliterate Roman Hindi before embedding queries
Add translated document copies only where a slice still falls short, then re-measure
pitfalls: An English-only model turns Devanagari into near-meaningless vectors
One overall recall number hides a failing language
Budgets and chunk sizes set on English undercount Hindi tokens
techniques.remember: One space for every language. Normalise the script, measure each slice.
techniques.cap: Illustrative: Kosh Bank, a fictional bank, whose support bot gets 50% English, 25% Hindi and 25% Hinglish queries.

cmp.best: Hinglish spelling varies; needs per-language tests

techniques.name: Late Interaction and Multi-Vector (ColBERT, ColPali)
techniques.q: Does one vector per passage lose too much detail?
techniques.what: Instead of squeezing each passage into one vector, late-interaction models keep a vector for every token. At query time each query token finds its best match among a passage’s token vectors, and those best matches are summed (MaxSim). ColBERT does this for text; ColPali does it for patches of page images, so scanned forms, tables and charts can be searched without OCR. Accuracy rises, especially on detail and visual documents, but the index is many times larger unless it is compressed.
use: Long or detailed passages where exact terms matter
Scanned forms, statements, tables and slides (ColPali)
A middle stage between fast retrieval and an expensive cross-encoder
metrics: one embedding per token or image patch, not one per passage
each query token takes its best match; the sum is the score
tens to hundreds of times a single vector, before compression
residual compression, pooling and binarisation shrink the index
page images in, patch vectors out: no OCR or layout parsing
steps: Decide where detail is lost: long passages, exact terms, visual pages
Index with ColBERT for text or ColPali for page images
Compress or pool the token vectors to keep the index affordable
Use it as a retriever or as a re-ranking stage over a cheaper first pass
pitfalls: Storing uncompressed multi-vectors and running out of memory
Using ColPali on clean digital text where text retrieval is cheaper
Skipping evaluation against a tuned single-vector baseline
techniques.remember: Keep every token, match each one, compress the index.
techniques.cap: Illustrative: Anand Bima, a fictional insurer, searches 10 lakh pages of claim documents, many of them scans.

from sentence_transformers import SentenceTransformer
import numpy as np

def chunk(text, size=200, overlap=40):                     #@1
    words = text.split()                                   #@1
    step = size - overlap                                  #@1
    return [" ".join(words[i:i + size]) for i in range(0, len(words), step)]   #@1

chunks = [c for doc in help_centre_docs for c in chunk(doc)]   #@1

model = SentenceTransformer("all-MiniLM-L6-v2")            #@2
doc_vecs = model.encode(chunks, normalize_embeddings=True)   # shape (n, 384)   #@2

query = "can I get my money back?"                         #@3
q = model.encode(query, normalize_embeddings=True)         #@3

scores = doc_vecs @ q          # unit vectors: dot product = cosine   #@4
top = np.argsort(-scores)[:2]                              #@5
for i in top:                                              #@5
    print(f"{scores[i]:.2f}  {chunks[i][:60]}")            #@5

def recall_at_k(eval_set, k=5):                            #@6
    hits = 0                                               #@6
    for question, gold_id in eval_set:                     #@6
        s = doc_vecs @ model.encode(question, normalize_embeddings=True)   #@6
        hits += gold_id in np.argsort(-s)[:k]              #@6
    return hits / len(eval_set)                            #@6
steps: Chunk the documents
Split each document into passages of about 200 words with a 40-word overlap, so no idea is cut at a boundary. One help article becomes three chunks.
Embed every chunk
The model turns each chunk into 384 numbers. Normalizing each vector to unit length lets a plain dot product act as cosine similarity.
Embed the query with the same model
The question goes through the same model. A vector from a different model lives in a different space and can’t be compared.
Score by cosine similarity
Compare the query vector with every chunk vector. The refunds chunk scores 0.71 even though it shares no words with the question.
Return the nearest neighbours
Sort by score and keep the top k. With k = 2 the two refund chunks come back; the shipping chunk at 0.22 does not.
Measure recall@k
Run 200 real questions with known answers and count how often the right chunk is in the top 5. Tune chunking and the model against this number.

import math
from collections import Counter

docs = [d.lower().split() for d in knowledge_base]         #@1
N = len(docs)                                              #@1
avgdl = sum(len(d) for d in docs) / N                      #@1,4
df = Counter(t for d in docs for t in set(d))              #@2

def idf(t):                                                #@2
    return math.log(1 + (N - df[t] + 0.5) / (df[t] + 0.5))   #@2

def bm25(query, doc, k1=1.2, b=0.75):                      #@3,4
    tf = Counter(doc)                                      #@3
    norm = k1 * (1 - b + b * len(doc) / avgdl)             #@4
    score = 0.0
    for t in query:
        f = tf[t]                                          #@3
        score += idf(t) * f * (k1 + 1) / (f + norm)        #@3,4
    return score

q = "E1045 login error".lower().split()                    #@1,5
bm25_rank = sorted(range(N), key=lambda i: bm25(q, docs[i]), reverse=True)   #@5

def rrf(rankings, k=60):                                   #@6
    fused = Counter()                                      #@6
    for ranking in rankings:                               #@6
        for r, doc_id in enumerate(ranking, start=1):      #@6
            fused[doc_id] += 1 / (k + r)                   #@6
    return [doc_id for doc_id, _ in fused.most_common()]   #@6

hybrid = rrf([bm25_rank, vector_rank])                     #@6
steps: Tokenize query and documents the same way
Lowercase and split both with one analyzer. “E1045 login error” becomes three terms: e1045, login and error.
Weigh each term by rarity (IDF)
Across 1,000 documents, e1045 appears in 3, login in 120 and error in 300. Rare terms get the most weight: IDF 5.66 versus 1.20.
Count term frequency, with saturation
More occurrences help, but with diminishing returns. With k1 = 1.2 a term’s contribution can never exceed 2.2 times its IDF.
Normalize for document length
b = 0.75 scales the saturation point by document length, so a 420-word post doesn’t win just by containing more words.
Rank the documents
Sum the term scores per document. The short runbook with e1045 scores 14.5; the long blog post without it scores 5.8.
Fuse with vector search
Reciprocal rank fusion adds 1 ÷ (60 + rank) from each list. Exact matches from BM25 and paraphrase matches from vectors both surface.

steps: Pick a model that covers both media
A CLIP-style model has an image encoder and a text encoder trained together, so both produce vectors in one space.
Embed the catalogue photos
Each product photo becomes one vector. A red shoe whose seller wrote only “New arrival, SKU 4471” is still findable by what it looks like.
Embed the text query
“red running shoe” goes through the text encoder and lands in the same space as the photos.
Compare across media
Cosine similarity works as usual. Scores of 0.31 and 0.29 look low, but text–image scores are low in general: the ranking is what counts.
Search by photo too
A customer’s photo goes through the image encoder and lands next to the same two red shoes: image-to-image search, same index.
Store links and test both directions
Keep each asset’s URL and caption as metadata, then test text-to-image and image-to-image queries on real examples.

from sentence_transformers.losses import MultipleNegativesRankingLoss
from sentence_transformers.training_args import BatchSamplers
from sentence_transformers.util import mine_hard_negatives

model = SentenceTransformer("BAAI/bge-small-en-v1.5")

pairs = Dataset.from_dict({"anchor": queries_from_search_logs,     #@1
                           "positive": clicked_articles})          #@1

train = mine_hard_negatives(pairs, model, range_min=10, range_max=50,   #@2
                            num_negatives=1)   # skip the top 10: likely true matches   #@2

loss = MultipleNegativesRankingLoss(model, scale=20.0)   # scale = 1 / temperature 0.05   #@3
args = SentenceTransformerTrainingArguments(                         #@3,4
    output_dir="bge-small-broking", num_train_epochs=1,              #@4
    per_device_train_batch_size=32,     # 31 in-batch negatives per query   #@3
    batch_sampler=BatchSamplers.NO_DUPLICATES)                       #@3
SentenceTransformerTrainer(model=model, args=args,                   #@4
                           train_dataset=train, loss=loss).train()   #@4

print(ir_evaluator(model))       # recall@10 on held-out real queries   #@5
print(ir_evaluator(SentenceTransformer("BAAI/bge-small-en-v1.5")))    #@5

new_vecs = model.encode(all_chunks, normalize_embeddings=True)       #@6

steps: Collect anchor–positive pairs
Take real signals: a search query and the article the user clicked, or a ticket and the answer that resolved it. “what is MTF” pairs with the MTF article.
Mine hard negatives
Search with the current model and pick a look-alike that is wrong, such as the mutual-fund article. Skip the very top hits: they are often true matches.
Use in-batch negatives and a temperature
With a batch of 32, each query also treats the other 31 positives as negatives. The loss is a softmax over similarities divided by the temperature τ = 0.05.
Train: pull in, push out
Each step raises the query’s similarity to its positive and lowers it for the hard negative, until the true match ranks first.
Evaluate on held-out queries
Compare recall@10 of the tuned and the base model on real queries the model never saw. Here it rises from 0.71 to 0.86.
Re-embed the corpus
A new model means a new vector space. Every stored chunk must be embedded again before the new model serves queries.

import numpy as np
from openai import OpenAI
client = OpenAI()

def embed(texts, dims):
    r = client.embeddings.create(model="text-embedding-3-small", input=texts,
                                 dimensions=dims)     # Matryoshka truncation   #@2
    return np.array([d.embedding for d in r.data], dtype=np.float32)

full = embed(chunks, 1536)                   # 1,536 × 4 B = 6,144 B each   #@1
base_recall = recall_at_k(full, eval_set, k=10)                             #@1

small = embed(chunks, 512)                   # 2,048 B each                 #@2

scale = np.abs(small).max(axis=0) / 127                                     #@3
small_i8 = np.round(small / scale).astype(np.int8)       # 512 B, 4x smaller   #@3

bits = np.packbits(full > 0, axis=1)         # 1,536 bits = 192 B, 32x smaller   #@4

def search_binary(q, k=10, oversample=4):                                    #@5
    qb = np.packbits(q > 0)                                                  #@5
    ham = np.unpackbits(bits ^ qb, axis=1).sum(axis=1)   # Hamming distance  #@5
    cand = np.argsort(ham)[:k * oversample]                                  #@5
    return cand[np.argsort(-(full[cand] @ q))][:k]   # rescore with float32  #@5

for name, idx in [("512 int8", small_i8), ("binary + rescore", bits)]:      #@6
    print(name, recall_at_k(idx, eval_set, k=10) / base_recall)             #@6
steps: Record the baseline
Measure recall@10 and memory at full size first: 1,536 float32 dimensions take 6,144 bytes per vector.
Truncate a Matryoshka model
Models trained Matryoshka-style put the most information in the first dimensions, so asking for 512 keeps about 99% of recall at a third of the size.
Quantize to int8
Store each value in 8 bits instead of 32 with a per-dimension scale: 512 bytes per vector, 4× smaller again, with a small recall loss.
Or go binary
Keep only the sign of each dimension: 1 bit each, 192 bytes for 1,536 dimensions, 32× smaller. On its own, recall falls to about 0.82.
Oversample, then rescore
Fetch 4× more candidates by fast Hamming distance, then rescore them with the full-precision vectors. Most of the lost recall comes back.
Choose by measured recall
Pick the smallest setting whose recall you can accept. Here 512-dimension int8 keeps 98% of recall at 12× less memory.

import re, unicodedata
import numpy as np
from sentence_transformers import SentenceTransformer

model = SentenceTransformer("intfloat/multilingual-e5-large")   # 1,024 dims, ~100 languages  #@1

DEVANAGARI = re.compile(r"[ऀ-ॿ]")
ROMAN_HINDI = {"paisa", "kab", "aayega", "kaise", "kyun", "nahi", "mera", "karo", "hai", "kya"}

def lang_of(text):                                                     #@2
    if DEVANAGARI.search(text):                                        #@2
        return "hi"
    words = set(re.findall(r"[a-z]+", text.lower()))
    return "hinglish" if len(words & ROMAN_HINDI) >= 2 else "en"       #@2

def normalise(text):                                                   #@3
    text = unicodedata.normalize("NFC", text)       # one byte form per letter  #@3
    if lang_of(text) == "hinglish":                                    #@3
        text = transliterate_roman_hindi(text)      # stub, e.g. IndicXlit; English words stay  #@3
    return text

docs = load_articles()                              # 2,40,000 English chunks  #@4
docs += [translate_to_hindi(d) for d in docs]       # optional Hindi copies, same ids  #@4
doc_vecs = model.encode(["passage: " + d["text"] for d in docs], normalize_embeddings=True)  #@1,4

def search(query, k=5):                                                #@5
    q = model.encode("query: " + normalise(query), normalize_embeddings=True)  #@1,5
    seen, hits = set(), []
    for i in np.argsort(-(doc_vecs @ q))[: 2 * k]:
        if docs[i]["id"] not in seen:               # an article and its copy count once  #@5
            seen.add(docs[i]["id"]); hits.append(docs[i])
    return hits[:k]

for lang in ["en", "hi", "hinglish"]:                                  #@6
    qs = [x for x in eval_set if lang_of(x["q"]) == lang]              #@6
    r = np.mean([x["gold"] in {d["id"] for d in search(x["q"])} for x in qs])
    print(lang, len(qs), f"recall@5 = {r:.0%}")                        #@6
steps: One model for every language

multilingual-e5-large maps about 100 languages, Hindi included, into one 1,024-dimension space. E5 models expect a “query: ” prefix on questions and a “passage: ” prefix on documents; skipping them quietly lowers recall.
Know each query's language

Devanagari is easy to spot from its Unicode block, U+0900 to U+097F. Hinglish is harder because it is plain ASCII; here two or more common Roman Hindi words mark it. In production a language-identification model does this job.
Normalise before embedding

Unicode NFC gives each Devanagari letter one byte form, so a nukta or vowel sign typed two ways embeds the same. Roman Hindi is then transliterated: “paisa kab aayega” becomes “पैसा कब आएगा”, while English words such as UPI stay as they are.
Decide what goes in the index

Kosh Bank, a fictional bank, has 2,40,000 English chunks. Adding a Hindi copy of each doubles the vectors to 4,80,000, and a Hindi chunk takes about 480 tokens against 300 for the English one, because Devanagari splits into more tokens.
Search once, count each article once

One search covers every language. Because an article and its Hindi copy can both score highly, the loop fetches 2k results and keeps the first hit per article id, so the top 5 holds five different articles.
Measure every language slice

Recall@5 is printed separately for English, Hindi and Hinglish. In the tuned setup that is 87%, 84% and 80%, so overall is 0.5 × 87 + 0.25 × 84 + 0.25 × 80 = 84.5%. With an English-only model the overall was 54.8%, which hid a Hindi slice at 8%.

ROMAN_HINDI = {"paisa", "kab", "aayega", "kaise", "nahi", "mera", "karo", "hai", "kya", "wapas"}
LEXICON = {"paisa": "पैसा", "kab": "कब", "aayega": "आएगा", "wapas": "वापस",
           "mera": "मेरा", "kya": "क्या", "hai": "है", "nahi": "नहीं"}

def normalise(text: str) -> str:
    text = unicodedata.normalize("NFC", text.strip())
    words = text.lower().split()
    if re.search(r"[ऀ-ॿ]", text) or len(set(words) & ROMAN_HINDI) < 2:
        return text                               # Devanagari or English: leave as typed
    return " ".join(LEXICON.get(w, w) for w in words)   # stub transliteration

articles = [
    ("A12", "Refunds for failed UPI payments reach your account within 5 working days."),
    ("A12", "विफल यूपीआई भुगतान का रिफंड 5 कार्यदिवसों में आपके खाते में आ जाता है।"),
    ("B07", "To block a lost debit card, open Cards and tap Block."),
]
ids = [a for a, _ in articles]
doc_vecs = model.encode([t for _, t in articles], normalize_embeddings=True)

def search(query: str, k: int = 5) -> list[str]:
    q = model.encode(normalise(query), normalize_embeddings=True)
    hits = []
    for i in np.argsort(-(doc_vecs @ q)):
        if ids[i] not in hits:                    # an article and its Hindi copy count once
            hits.append(ids[i])
    return hits[:k]

for q in ["when will my refund come", "पैसा कब आएगा", "upi fail hua paisa kab aayega"]:
    print(q, "->", search(q, k=1))

scores = doc_vecs @ q
top5 = np.argsort(-scores)[:5]
semantic.explain: The query is embedded with a different model from the documents. Both output 384 numbers, so nothing crashes, but the two vector spaces are unrelated and the scores are noise. Queries and documents must use the same model.

also.2: Loading a second model is harmless on its own. The mistake is where it gets used.
also.5: Both sides are normalized, so the dot product is the cosine similarity. This line is fine.

bm25.title: Inverse document frequency
bm25.explain: The fraction is upside down. BM25’s IDF is ln(1 + (N − df + 0.5) ÷ (df + 0.5)), which is large for rare terms. As written, a term in 3 of 1,000 documents gets almost no weight and “the” gets the most.

multimodal.title: Text-to-image product search
multimodal.code:
model = SentenceTransformer("clip-ViT-B-32")
img_vecs = model.encode([Image.open(p) for p in paths], normalize_embeddings=True)
q = model.encode("red running shoe", normalize_embeddings=True)
scores = img_vecs @ q
hits = [p for p, s in zip(paths, scores) if s > 0.8]   # threshold from our text search
multimodal.explain: Text-to-image cosine similarities in CLIP-style models are typically around 0.2 to 0.35, even for good matches, so a 0.8 threshold copied from text search returns nothing. Rank the results and take the top k, or tune a threshold for this model on your own data.

also.3: Encoding the text with the same CLIP model is exactly right: its text encoder shares the space with the image encoder.

contrastive.title: Mining hard negatives
contrastive.explain: The top results for a query very often include the positive itself or other true matches. Using them as negatives teaches the model to push correct answers away. Remove the positive and skip the very top ranks, or filter candidates with a cross-encoder.
contrastive.fix: hard_negs = [c for c in candidates if c != positive][2:5]

also.3: Mining candidates with the current retriever is the standard way to find hard negatives.

dimred.title: Searching truncated Matryoshka vectors
dimred.code:
full = model.encode(chunks, normalize_embeddings=True)    # 1,024 dims, unit length
small = full[:, :256]                                      # keep the first 256
q = model.encode(query, normalize_embeddings=True)[:256]
scores = small @ q                                         # cosine similarity
dimred.explain: After truncation the vectors are no longer unit length, so the dot product is not the cosine similarity: vectors with more of their length in the first 256 dimensions get an unfair boost. Re-normalize after truncating, or divide by the norms.

also.2: Keeping the first dimensions is exactly how Matryoshka truncation works.

multiling.title: Hinglish mistaken for English
multiling.explain: Hinglish such as “paisa kab aayega” is plain ASCII, so it returns early and is never transliterated, while Devanagari queries, which are not ASCII, are sent to a Roman-to-Devanagari transliterator that has nothing to do. The check tests the character set, not the language.

also.2: Correct: NFC gives each Devanagari letter one byte form before anything else happens.

lateint.title: Scoring with late interaction
lateint.explain: Averaging every query–document pair blurs the signal: most pairs are unrelated. MaxSim takes each query token’s best match and sums those.

also.2: Normalised vectors make the dot product a cosine similarity, which is right.

2: Each chunk now goes through the embedding model. What comes out?
A fixed-length vector of numbers for each chunk
A list of the chunk’s keywords with weights
A dense model outputs a fixed-length vector, here 384 numbers, whatever the chunk says.
3: Which model should embed the customer’s question?
Any model with the same number of dimensions
The same model used for the chunks
Only the same model puts queries and documents in the same vector space.
4: The question shares no words with the refund chunk. How does it score?
Near zero: there is nothing to match
High, because the meanings are close
Dense vectors capture meaning, so a paraphrase scores high without shared words.
5: Scores are 0.71, 0.58 and 0.22 and k = 2. Which chunks come back?
The two refund chunks
All three, because every score is positive
Top-k keeps the k highest scores: 0.71 and 0.58.
6: How do you know whether chunking and the model are good enough?
Check that the top scores are above 0.9
Measure recall@k on real questions with known answers
Absolute scores vary by model; recall@k on real questions measures what users experience.

2: Which query term gets the largest IDF weight?
error, because it appears in the most documents
e1045, because it appears in the fewest
IDF rewards rarity: e1045 is in 3 of 1,000 documents.
3: A term appears 12 times instead of once. Does its contribution grow 12×?
Yes, term frequency is linear
No, it saturates, controlled by k1
The tf part is f × (k1 + 1) ÷ (f + norm), which levels off as f grows.
4: Two documents contain the same matches; one is 10× longer. With b = 0.75, which scores higher?
The shorter one
They score the same
Length normalization raises the saturation point for long documents, so the same matches count for less.
5: Which document ranks first for “E1045 login error”?
The long blog post that repeats login and error
The short runbook that contains e1045
The rare code carries so much IDF weight that the runbook wins, 14.5 to 5.8.
6: How does reciprocal rank fusion combine BM25 and vector results?
It adds 1 ÷ (k + rank) from each list
It averages the raw scores
RRF uses ranks, not scores, so it needs no calibration between very different scoring scales.

2: A red shoe’s description says only “SKU 4471”. Can a text query still find it?
Yes, if its photo is embedded in the shared space
No, the text is all the index has
The photo vector carries what the product looks like, whatever the description says.
3: Which encoder embeds the text query “red running shoe”?
The model’s text encoder, into the same space as the images
A separate text-only embedding model
Only the paired text encoder produces vectors comparable with the image vectors.
4: The best matches score 0.31 and 0.29. Is something wrong?
Yes, good matches should score above 0.8
No, text–image scores are low in general; the ranking matters
Cross-modal cosines are low in absolute terms; set thresholds per model, or just rank.
5: Can the same index answer a customer’s photo?
No, you need a second index for photo queries
Yes, the photo goes through the image encoder
Image-to-image search uses the same vectors and the same similarity.
6: What should each vector’s metadata include?
A link to the original asset and its caption
Nothing: the vector is enough
Results must link back to the product and its text, which also allows hybrid filtering.

2: Which makes the most useful negative for “what is MTF”?
A random article about login problems
The mutual-fund article that looks similar
Hard negatives, which look right but are wrong, teach the distinctions the model is missing.
3: With a batch of 32 pairs, how many in-batch negatives does each query get?
Every other positive in the batch acts as a negative: 32 − 1 = 31.
4: What does each training step do to the similarities?
Raises the positive’s and lowers the hard negative’s
Raises both, since both are relevant-looking
The contrastive loss pulls the true pair together and pushes the negatives apart.
5: Where do you measure the improvement?
On the training pairs
On held-out real queries the model never saw
Training pairs reward memorization; held-out queries show real retrieval gains.
6: The tuned model is better. Can you use it on the existing index?
Yes, queries just use the new model
No, every chunk must be re-embedded first
New model, new vector space: old document vectors can’t be compared with new query vectors.

2: You keep the first 512 of 1,536 dimensions of a Matryoshka model. What happens to recall?
It stays close to the baseline
It falls by about two thirds
Matryoshka training puts the most information first, so truncation loses little. A model not trained this way would lose far more.
3: int8 stores each value in 8 bits. How much smaller than float32?
32 bits ÷ 8 bits = 4×.
4: Binary keeps 1 bit per dimension. How many bytes for 1,536 dimensions?
1,536 bits ÷ 8 = 192 bytes, 32× smaller than float32.
5: Binary search alone loses recall. What brings most of it back?
Using more bits for the query only
Fetching more candidates and rescoring them with full-precision vectors
Oversample with the cheap vectors, then re-sort the candidates precisely.
6: Which setting should you ship?
The smallest one whose measured recall meets your target
Always binary, because it is smallest
The right trade-off depends on your recall target and memory budget, so measure.

2: A query reads “mera card block karo”. Which label does lang_of give it?
en, because it is all ASCII
hinglish, because it contains Roman Hindi words
“mera” and “karo” are both in the Roman Hindi word list, so two matches mark it as Hinglish even though every character is ASCII.
3: What does transliteration do to “paisa kab aayega”?
Translates it into English
Rewrites the Hindi words in Devanagari: पैसा कब आएगा
Transliteration changes the script, not the language. English words in the query, such as UPI, stay as typed.
4: Kosh Bank adds a Hindi copy of each of its 2,40,000 chunks. What happens to the index?
It doubles to 4,80,000 vectors, and each Hindi chunk costs more tokens to embed
Nothing: the model stores one vector per meaning
Each copy is a separate vector. At about 480 tokens against 300 for English, the copies add 11,52,00,000 tokens.
5: An article and its Hindi copy both reach the top 5. What does the search loop do?
Keeps both, since they are different texts
Counts the article once and fills the slot with the next result
Recall@5 is about finding the right article; two copies of it in the top 5 would crowd out a different useful result.
6: Overall recall@5 is 54.8% with the English-only model. What should you check next?
Recall for each language separately
A larger k
The 54.8% is 0.5 × 88% + 0.25 × 8% + 0.25 × 35%: English is fine and Hindi is almost never served.

2: A scanned hospital bill is indexed with ColQwen. Is OCR needed?
No: the page image is embedded directly
Yes: images must be OCRed first
ColPali-family models read page patches.
3: How is a page scored for “total”?
The best-matching patch for each query token, summed
The average of all patches
MaxSim takes each token’s best match.
4: The raw index is 260 GB. What brings it down?
Pooling and binarising patch vectors
Deleting half the pages
Compression keeps most accuracy at a fraction of the size.
5: Where else can late interaction sit?
As a re-ranker over a cheaper first stage
Only as the first stage
Re-ranking limits the multi-vector cost to a small candidate set.
6: On clean text only, what gain would you expect?
Smaller than on scans
Larger than on scans
The biggest wins are on visual pages that OCR mangles.

semantic: Text becomes a dense vector of numbers.
Similar meaning lands close together, even without shared words.
Search ranks chunks by similarity to the query vector.
Documents are split into passages before embedding.
the same model for queries and documents
Queries and documents must share one model and space.
measuring recall or the exact-term weakness
Measure recall@k, and remember that exact codes need keyword search.
bm25: It matches the exact words in the query.
Rare terms weigh more than common ones.
Pair it with dense vectors in a hybrid search.
multimodal: It covers images and other media, not just text.
Text and images land in one space.
A text query can find an image and the reverse.
Trained by aligning images with their captions.
Small printed text and exact counts are often lost.
Text–image scores are low; rank rather than threshold.
contrastive: It is how embedding models are trained and adapted.
True matches move closer and wrong ones move away.
Look-alike wrong answers teach the most.
The loss is a softmax over similarities, with in-batch negatives and a temperature.
Check held-out recall, then re-embed the corpus.
dimred: To save memory, storage and cost.
Keep the first dimensions of a model trained for it.
Store each value in fewer bits.
Fetch extra candidates, then rescore with full vectors.
Recall drops a little, so measure it.
multiling: Every language is embedded into one shared space.
Use a model trained on many languages.
A Hindi query can find an English document.
Normalise Unicode and transliterate Roman Hindi.
Report recall for each language slice.
Hindi text costs more tokens, and copies double the index.
lateint: One vector per token or image patch.
Each query token takes its best match; sum them.
ColPali searches page images without OCR.

semantic: Customers search “money deducted twice”. The right article is titled “Duplicate debit reversal”, and keyword search finds nothing. What helps most?
The query and title share no words but mean the same thing. Dense embeddings match meaning.
Two symptom notes embed as a = [3, 4] and b = [4, 3]. What is their cosine similarity?
Product search quality is poor after launch. Which of these could be causing it? Select all that apply.
Documents were embedded with one model and queries with another
Chunks cut specification tables in half
Cosine similarity is computed on normalized vectors
Most queries are bare SKU codes
Mismatched models, broken chunks and code-only queries all hurt dense search. Cosine on normalized vectors is correct.
The team switched embedding models for new policy documents only; old documents keep their old vectors. What happens to searches over old documents?
They improve, because queries use the better model
Scores against old vectors become meaningless
Nothing changes while the dimensions match
Only the similarity threshold needs lowering
Different models produce unrelated vector spaces. Re-embed the whole corpus when you change models.
On 200 test questions, the right chunk appears in the top 5 for 168 of them. What is recall@5?
Why is a bi-encoder, not a cross-encoder, used to search 10 million help-centre chunks?
Document vectors can be computed once, ahead of time
A bi-encoder embeds documents independently, so search is a fast vector comparison. A cross-encoder must read every query–document pair.
A firm embeds each 12,000-word contract as a single vector, and clause questions retrieve the wrong contracts. What is the best fix?
Chunk on clause and section boundaries with a little overlap
Use a larger embedding model on whole contracts
One vector for a whole contract blurs every clause together. Chunks of a few hundred tokens keep each clause findable.
What should you store next to each chunk vector in the index? Select all that apply.
The float values again as a text string
Metadata lets you cite, filter by date or course, and enforce permissions. Duplicating the vector as text adds nothing.
Both vectors are normalized to unit length and their dot product is 0.83. What is their cosine similarity?
For unit vectors cosine = a · b ÷ (1 × 1), so it equals the dot product.
5 million chunks are embedded at 768 float32 dimensions. How much memory do the raw vectors need?
768 × 4 B = 3,072 B per vector × 5 million ≈ 15.4 GB.
Passengers write to support in Hindi, Tamil and English. How should you choose the embedding model?
Pick the model with the most dimensions
Shortlist multilingual models and compare recall on real queries in each language
Translate everything to English and use any model
Language coverage varies by model. Measure on your own queries, per language.
After switching models, a similarity threshold of 0.8 that worked before now returns almost nothing. Why?
Score ranges differ between models, so thresholds must be re-tuned
The index needs rebuilding with more shards
Each model spreads its scores differently. Tune thresholds per model on your own data, or rely on ranking.
A hospital is choosing an embedding model for clinical guideline search. Which steps are sound? Select all that apply.
Build a labelled set of real clinician questions
Compare recall@k of each candidate on that set
Pick the model with the largest vectors
Public benchmarks shortlist; your own labelled questions decide. Vector size alone says little about quality.
Exact nearest-neighbour search over 200 million vectors takes seconds per query. What is the standard remedy?
An approximate nearest-neighbour index such as HNSW
ANN indexes trade a little recall for orders-of-magnitude faster search.
The team uses an E5 model but embeds queries and products with no prefixes, and quality is lower than published results. What is the likely fix?
Add the “query: ” and “passage: ” prefixes the model was trained with
E5 models expect these prefixes. Follow the model card’s input format.
Besides search, what else can the same claim-description embeddings do well?
Flag near-duplicate claims by very high cosine similarity
Embeddings support clustering, deduplication and recommendations, not arithmetic or OCR.
Why add a 40-word overlap between consecutive 200-word chunks?
So an idea split at a boundary still appears whole in one chunk
To make every chunk the same vector
Overlap reduces the chance that the sentence answering a question is cut in half.
Which queries are likely to fail with dense-only search? Select all that apply.
“my internet is really slow at night”
Reference numbers and IMEIs are exact tokens with little meaning. Natural-language questions suit dense search.
What is the cosine similarity of a = [1, 0, 1] and b = [0, 1, 1]?
A résumé-search index holds 1 million embedded chunks, and 5,000 new résumés arrive daily. The model is unchanged. What should you do?
Embed only the new résumés with the same model and add them
Re-embed all 1 million chunks every day
Embed new résumés with the newest model available
Re-embedding everything is needed only when the model changes. New content just needs the same model.
bm25: Engineers search for “ERR_ORD_1045”, and vector search returns generic error articles. What is the fix?
Add BM25 and fuse it with vector search
Rare exact tokens are BM25’s strength. Hybrid search keeps both kinds of match.
A term appears in 10 of 10,000 case files. Using IDF = ln(N ÷ df), what is its IDF?
Why does the word “the” add almost nothing to a product’s BM25 score?
It is filtered by length normalization
Its IDF is tiny because it appears in almost every document
It is shorter than four characters
IDF rewards rare terms; a word in every document carries no signal.
Which setups can make BM25 miss documents that do contain the query terms? Select all that apply.
The index lowercases text but the query does not
Stemming is applied at index time but not at query time
The same analyzer is used for index and query
“UPI-ID” is split into different tokens at index and query time
Index and query must be tokenized identically. The same analyzer on both sides is the fix, not a cause.
What happens to BM25 scoring when k1 = 0?
Only whether a term appears matters, not how often
With k1 = 0 the term-frequency factor is 1 for any f > 0, so repeats add nothing.
A news archive sets b = 0. What changes?
Document length no longer affects scores, so long articles gain
b controls length normalization; b = 0 switches it off.
With k1 = 1.2 and a document of average length (b has no effect), what is the term-frequency factor f × (k1 + 1) ÷ (f + k1) for f = 3?
With k1 = 1.2, what is the most a single term’s frequency factor can ever reach, however often it repeats?
f × (k1 + 1) ÷ (f + k1 × (1 − b + b × len ÷ avgdl)) approaches k1 + 1 = 2.2 as f grows.
Which queries are better served by BM25 than by dense vectors? Select all that apply.
Drug names, codes and record numbers are exact tokens. The symptom description is a meaning query.
A document is ranked 1st by BM25 and 3rd by vector search. With RRF and k = 60, what is its fused score?
Why fuse BM25 and vector results with reciprocal rank fusion instead of adding the raw scores?
RRF is more accurate by definition
The two scores are on very different, uncalibrated scales
Raw scores cannot be added in Python
BM25 scores are unbounded while cosine lies in [−1, 1]. RRF uses only ranks, so no calibration is needed.
A search for “car accident” misses judgments that only say “motor vehicle collision”. What addresses this?
Adding dense retrieval or learned sparse expansion alongside BM25
BM25 has no notion of synonyms. Dense vectors or a learned sparse model such as SPLADE add them.
Matches in shipment-manual titles matter more than matches in the body. What is the standard approach?
Index title and body as separate fields and boost the title
Repeat the title ten times in the body
Remove the body from the index
Per-field indexing with boosts expresses importance without distorting term frequencies.
Which statements describe SPLADE? Select all that apply.
It can add relevant terms the text does not contain
It can be served from an inverted index like BM25
SPLADE learns term weights and expansions but keeps the sparse, inverted-index form.
A payments team already runs Postgres and needs basic keyword search over dispute notes with no new infrastructure. Which tool fits?
Postgres full-text search runs next to the data. Note that its ts_rank ranking is not BM25.
A BM25 search for booking reference “X7K2PQ” misses a document that contains it. What is the most likely cause?
The IDF of the code is too high
Index and query analyzers tokenize the code differently
Codes are fragile under tokenization. Use the same analyzer, or a keyword field that keeps the code intact.
With b = 0.75, a 300-word document and an average length of 150 words, what is the length factor 1 − b + b × len ÷ avgdl?
A seller repeats “iphone” 50 times in a listing. Which part of BM25 limits the benefit?
Each extra occurrence adds less, so stuffing gains little beyond the first few repeats.
Which statements about IDF are true? Select all that apply.
Rare terms get a higher IDF
A term in every document gets an IDF close to 0 with Lucene’s formula
IDF depends on the length of the query
IDF is computed across the whole collection
IDF measures rarity across the collection; the query length does not affect it.
You are building a test set to compare BM25-only with hybrid search. What should it include? Select all that apply.
Queries containing error codes and ISINs
The known correct documents for every query
Only queries that already succeed today
Cover both failure types, with labelled answers. Only-successful queries hide the problems.
multimodal: Customers upload photos of broken parts to find the right spare. Which technique fits?
Photos and product listings need to share one vector space.
An insurer wants to find past claims whose damage photos look like a new one. How?
Embed claim photos with an image encoder and search image-to-image
Ask an LLM to describe the photo and search for the exact caption
Image-to-image search compares photo vectors directly in the same space.
Which statements about CLIP-style models are true? Select all that apply.
The image and text encoders are trained together
In the original CLIP models, matching text–image cosine scores are typically low, around 0.2 to 0.35
They read small serial numbers reliably
CLIP aligns images and captions; its scores are low in absolute terms, and fine printed detail is a known weakness.
A 0.8 similarity threshold copied from text search returns no products for text-to-image queries. What do you do?
Rank and keep the top k, or tune a threshold for this model
Cross-modal scores are low for everyone. The ranking is what carries the signal.
A bank must search thousands of scanned KYC forms full of tables and stamps. Which approach fits?
OCR and layout parsing, or page-image retrieval such as ColPali
A text-only model on the file names
Either extract the text or embed the page images; many systems combine both.
2 million images are embedded at 512 float32 dimensions. How much memory do the vectors need?
A red running shoe is listed as “New arrival, SKU 4471”, and text search never shows it for “red running shoe”. What fixes this?
Index product photos with a multimodal model
Its photo carries what the description lacks.
Which are real risks when using general image embeddings on patient photos? Select all that apply.
Clinical images differ from web photos, so quality can drop
Embedding patient photos brings privacy and consent obligations
General models always beat specialist ones
Domain shift, lost detail and data protection are the main concerns; specialist models often do better.
Buyers type “sunny balcony with plants” to search listing photos. What kind of search is this?
Text-to-image search in a shared space
The text encoder embeds the query; it is compared with photo vectors.
Students search lecture slides where the answer is in a diagram with a short caption. What fits best?
A model that embeds slide images or mixed text and images
A text model on file names
Slides carry meaning in their visuals, so embed the rendered slide, not just its text.
Text-to-text and text-to-image scores are merged by raw value, and photo matches never appear. Why?
Text–text scores sit on a higher scale, so they always win
Photos cannot be searched with text
Cosine similarity is undefined for images
Normalize each list or merge by rank, for example with reciprocal rank fusion.
Shoppers search one catalogue in Hindi, Tamil and English, by text or photo. What should you look for?
A multilingual multimodal model, with a licence that allows commercial use
Language coverage and licence both matter; some open multilingual weights are non-commercial.
What should each image vector’s metadata include? Select all that apply.
The URL of the original image
Metadata links results back to products and enables filtering. Pixels belong in object storage.
Engineers search drawings by exact part numbers printed on them. What should you add to image embeddings?
OCR the drawings and index the text with BM25
Image embeddings lose small printed text; OCR plus keyword search catches exact numbers.
A 2-hour video is sampled at one frame every 2 seconds for embedding. How many frames is that?
7,200 seconds ÷ 2 = 3,600 frames, each linked to its timestamp.
Photos were embedded with a CLIP image encoder, but queries use a separate sentence-transformers text model. What happens?
Scores are meaningless, because the vectors come from unrelated spaces
It works if the dimensions match
Results improve because the text model is stronger
Only the paired text encoder produces vectors in the image encoder’s space.
Which checks belong in a multimodal search evaluation? Select all that apply.
Fine-detail queries, to confirm text indexing covers them
Only checking that the average cosine is above 0.5
Test each direction and the known weak spot. Average scores say nothing about ranking quality.
Which of these are cross-modal searches? Select all that apply.
A text query that retrieves product photos
A photo that retrieves a manual page
A text question that retrieves a text FAQ
A photo of router lights that retrieves a troubleshooting article
Cross-modal means the query and result are different media.
A general CLIP model ranks dermatology photos poorly. What is the most promising next step?
Fine-tune on labelled domain image–text pairs, or use a domain-specific model
Convert the photos to binary vectors
Domain shift is fixed with domain data, often through contrastive fine-tuning.
How does SigLIP’s training differ from the original CLIP?
It uses a pairwise sigmoid loss instead of a softmax over the batch
It uses BM25 scores as labels
SigLIP scores each image–text pair independently with a sigmoid loss.
contrastive: Your embeddings treat “MTF” and “MF” as nearly identical. What is the best long-term fix?
Training on real query–article pairs with look-alike wrong answers teaches the distinction.
A batch holds 64 (query, positive) pairs. With in-batch negatives, how many negatives does each query see?
Every other positive in the batch acts as a negative: 64 − 1 = 63.
Which are good sources of positive training pairs? Select all that apply.
Search query → clicked article the user stayed on
Support ticket → the knowledge-base article that resolved it
Real signals of relevance make good positives. Random pairs are not matches.
Mined “negatives” often turn out to be clauses that also answer the query. What does this do, and what is the fix?
It teaches the model to push true matches away; filter candidates or skip the top ranks
Nothing: more negatives are always better
It speeds up training; keep them
False negatives confuse training. Remove likely positives, for example with a cross-encoder.
Which make a sound evaluation of a fine-tuned embedding model? Select all that apply.
Held-out real queries never used in training
A comparison with the base model on the same set
A check that general queries did not get worse
Training pairs reward memorization. Held-out data and a baseline show real gains.
MultipleNegativesRankingLoss uses scale = 20. Which temperature does that correspond to?
A query has similarity 0.8 to its positive and 0.6 to one negative, with τ = 0.1. What probability does the softmax give the positive?
Which are warning signs of overfitting during fine-tuning? Select all that apply.
In-domain recall rises but general queries degrade
Training loss is near zero while held-out recall is flat
Held-out recall and general queries both improve
Memorizing a small set shows up as a gap between training and held-out results.
The fine-tuned model beats the base model. What must happen before it serves queries?
Re-embed every document with the new model
Nothing: swap the query model only
A new model means a new vector space; old document vectors are not comparable.
Why use a batch sampler that avoids duplicate texts within a batch?
A duplicate would act as a negative for its own match
It removes the need for positives
If the same text appears twice, in-batch negatives include a true match, creating a false negative.
Training uses only random easy negatives. The loss is near zero, but look-alike articles still outrank the right ones. Why?
Easy negatives are already far away, so there is almost nothing to learn
The learning rate is too high
The batch is too small to compute a loss
The model has too many dimensions
Without hard negatives, the loss never sees the confusions that matter.
Training with temperature 1.0 separates matches from non-matches only weakly. Why?
Dividing similarities by a large temperature flattens the softmax
A temperature of 1 disables the loss
Low temperatures such as 0.05 turn small similarity gaps into large probability gaps.
Which are good practices for mining hard negatives? Select all that apply.
Mine them with the current retriever
Filter candidates with a cross-encoder to remove true matches
Use the positive itself as a negative
Look-alikes come from your retriever; filtering removes false negatives.
Which of these is trained with a contrastive objective?
CLIP aligns image–caption pairs contrastively. The others involve no such training.
A team has 150 query–article pairs and wants to fine-tune. What is the best advice?
Collect thousands of real pairs first; 150 invites overfitting
Train for 50 epochs to make up for it
Skip evaluation because the data is small
Small datasets overfit easily. Gather more signal and keep a held-out set.
You only have (anchor, positive) pairs, with no labelled negatives. Which loss suits this?
A triplet loss that needs an explicit negative
Mean squared error on raw text
It treats the other positives in the batch as negatives.
On 200 held-out queries, the base model finds the answer in the top 10 for 142 and the tuned model for 172. What changed?
Which click signals are noisy and need filtering before training? Select all that apply.
Clicks on rank 1 driven by position
Short visits, position bias and bots are not relevance. Purchases are strong positives.
Re-embedding 12 million chunks runs at 2,000 chunks per second. How long does it take?
You want to fine-tune a BGE model with the recipes used to train it. Which tool fits?
FlagEmbedding is BAAI’s library for training and fine-tuning BGE models.
dimred: 30 million vectors × 1,024 float32 dimensions. How much memory do the raw vectors need?
The same 30 million × 1,024 vectors are quantized to int8. How much memory now?
100 million vectors of 1,024 dimensions are binary quantized. How much memory?
Which statements about Matryoshka embeddings are true? Select all that apply.
The model is trained so the first dimensions carry the most information
Truncating a model not trained this way loses much more quality
Vectors should be re-normalized after truncation before cosine search
Each truncation size needs a retrained model
One Matryoshka model supports many sizes; you just keep the first dimensions and re-normalize.
Binary quantization cut memory 32×, but recall dropped. What is the standard remedy?
Oversample candidates and rescore them with full-precision vectors
Fetch more cheap candidates, then re-sort them precisely: most recall comes back.
A UMAP plot of note embeddings shows two diagnoses overlapping. What should you conclude?
Nothing firm: 2-D projections distort distances, so measure retrieval directly
Search will fail for both diagnoses
UMAP and t-SNE are for inspection, not proof. Check recall on real queries.
1,536 float32 dimensions are reduced to 256 dimensions in int8. How much smaller is each vector?
You use OpenAI text-embedding-3-small and want 512-dimension vectors without training anything. How?
Pass dimensions=512 in the embeddings request
Run PCA on each single vector
text-embedding-3 models support a dimensions parameter because they were trained Matryoshka-style.
Which statements about product quantization are true? Select all that apply.
It splits each vector into sub-vectors
It stores a codebook ID for each sub-vector
Its codebooks are learned from the data
PQ compresses heavily by approximating sub-vectors with learned centroids, so some accuracy is lost.
Your embedding model was not trained Matryoshka-style, and you need 256 dimensions. What is the better option?
Fit PCA on a sample and project, then measure recall, or switch to a Matryoshka model
Keep the first 256 values and assume nothing changes
Round values to one decimal place
Naive truncation discards information spread across all dimensions in such a model.
You need the top 10 results and oversample 4× before rescoring. How many candidates are rescored?
A newsroom index holds 200,000 vectors at 768 float32 dimensions on a 16 GB server. Should you compress?
Probably not: about 614 MB already fits comfortably
768 × 4 B = 3,072 B × 200,000 ≈ 614 MB. Compression would cost recall for no gain.
What should you measure before and after compressing an index? Select all that apply.
Compression trades recall for memory and speed. Measure all three.
How many bytes does a 1,536-dimension float16 vector take?
In a binary index with rescoring, where do the full-precision vectors usually live?
On disk or cheaper storage, read only for the candidates
In RAM next to the binary vectors, always
RAM holds the compact index; the full vectors are fetched only to rescore a few candidates.
Which practices make int8 quantization safer? Select all that apply.
Calibrate value ranges on a representative sample
Keep the float32 originals for rescoring
Compute the scale from a single vector
A range taken from one vector clips values in others. Calibrate, measure and keep originals.
Which of these reduce the memory an index needs? Select all that apply.
More overlap creates more chunks, which increases memory.
A team truncated a 1,024-dimension model that was not trained Matryoshka-style to 128 dimensions, and recall collapsed. Why?
Its information is spread across all dimensions, so the first 128 lose most of it
128 is below the minimum any database accepts
Cosine similarity needs at least 256 dimensions
Only Matryoshka-trained models concentrate information in the first dimensions.
What is the Hamming distance between binary codes 1011 and 1101?
They differ in the second and third positions: distance 2.
You want binary quantization with oversampling and rescoring configured per collection, without custom code. Which tool fits?
Qdrant supports scalar, binary and product quantization with rescoring settings.
multiling: A bank’s help articles are all in English. A customer asks “पैसा कब आएगा” and an English-only embedding model returns nothing useful. What is the most direct fix?
Switch to a multilingual embedding model so Hindi and English share one vector space
Add more English synonyms to the articles
An English-only model has almost no Hindi in its vocabulary, so Devanagari becomes near-meaningless vectors. A multilingual model places the Hindi query near the English article.
Queries are 50% English, 25% Hindi and 25% Hinglish. Recall@5 is 88%, 8% and 35%. What is overall recall@5?
Why is the 54.75% in the previous question a poor thing to put on a dashboard alone?
It hides that Hindi queries almost never find the right article
Hinglish should be excluded from evaluation
A weighted average lets the large English slice mask a failing Hindi slice at 8%. Report each language separately.
What does transliteration do to “paisa kab aayega”?
Translates it to “when will the money come”
Rewrites it in Devanagari as “पैसा कब आएगा”
Transliteration changes the script, not the language. Translation would change the language.
A normalise() function skips transliteration whenever query.isascii() is true. Which queries are handled wrongly?
Hinglish queries in Roman script, which are also ASCII
Roman Hindi is plain ASCII, so it is treated as English and never transliterated. Detect the language, not the character set.
An insurer indexes 1,50,000 English chunks and adds a Hindi copy of each, using a 1,024-dimension float32 model. How large is the raw vector index?
3,00,000 vectors × 1,024 dims × 4 B = 1,228,800,000 B ≈ 1.23 GB. Without the copies it would be about 614 MB.
English chunks average 300 tokens and the Hindi translations take 1.6 times as many. How many tokens do 2,40,000 Hindi copies add?
Which are real multilingual embedding options as of 2026? Select all that apply.
all-MiniLM-L6-v2 is an English sentence-transformers model. BGE-M3, multilingual-e5 and Cohere’s multilingual models cover about 100 languages.
A hospital uses intfloat/multilingual-e5-large but embeds queries and passages as raw text. What is likely wrong?
E5 expects “query: ” and “passage: ” prefixes; leaving them out lowers retrieval quality
E5 models were trained with these prefixes, and the model card asks for them. BGE-M3, by contrast, needs no query instruction.
Two copies of the same refund article, English and Hindi, both appear in a customer’s top 5. What should the search do?
Keep both, as they are different texts
De-duplicate by article id and fill the slot with the next distinct article
Drop the Hindi copy from the index
Fetch a few extra candidates and keep one hit per article id, so the top 5 holds five different answers.
A shopper types “लाल kurta cotton”. Which describes this query?
Code-mixed: Devanagari Hindi and Roman-script words in one query
Mixing scripts and languages within one query is common in India; the model and normalisation must handle both parts.
Kosh Bank’s Hinglish slice is at 58% with a multilingual model. Which steps are likely to raise it? Select all that apply.
Transliterate Roman Hindi to Devanagari before embedding
Add Hindi copies of the articles
Collect real Hinglish queries to test on
Transliteration and Hindi copies both helped in the playground (72% and 80%); real Hinglish test queries tell you whether they work on your data. An English-only model makes it worse.
Why do Hindi documents usually cost more to embed than English documents of the same meaning?
Devanagari usually splits into more tokens per word
Hindi text must be embedded twice
APIs charge more per Hindi token by rule
Tokenizers trained mostly on English break Devanagari into more pieces, so tokenizer fertility, and so cost and chunk length, rise.
A Hindi slice has 250 test queries and the right article appears in the top 5 for 210 of them. What is Hindi recall@5?
Hindi is 25% of traffic. Hindi recall rises from 74% to 84% while other slices stay the same. How much does overall recall rise?
Why apply Unicode NFC normalisation to Devanagari text before embedding?
So the same letter typed in two byte forms, such as a nukta letter, embeds the same way
Some Devanagari letters have precomposed and decomposed forms. NFC picks one, so identical-looking text gives identical input.
Which belong in a good multilingual retrieval test set? Select all that apply.
Real Hindi and Hinglish queries from logs, labelled by language
Several spellings of common Hinglish words, such as aayega and ayega
Only English queries machine-translated into Hindi
The correct article id for each query
Machine-translated English is cleaner than what customers type and misses code-mixing; use real queries with gold answers.
Which tool is built for transliterating Roman script into Indian scripts?
IndicXlit, trained on the Aksharantar dataset, transliterates between Roman script and 21 Indic languages.
A search index serves only English queries over English documents. Is a multilingual model worth it?
Usually not: an English-only model may be a little better and smaller
Always: multilingual models are better at English
Yes, because it halves the index size
Yes, because it removes the need for evaluation
Multilingual models spread capacity over many languages. With no other languages in play, compare both on your English queries.
Which statements about cross-lingual retrieval with a multilingual model are true? Select all that apply.
A Hindi query can find an English article with no translation step
Recall for Hindi queries is often lower than for English queries on English documents
Translated copies of documents can close part of the gap
It removes the need to evaluate each language
Cross-lingual matching works but usually trails same-language matching; translated copies help, and each language still needs its own evaluation.
lateint: What does late interaction keep that a single-vector model does not?
A vector per token or patch
How is a MaxSim score computed?
Sum over query tokens of each token’s best match
Best match per query token, summed.
Which documents benefit most from ColPali?
Scanned forms, bills, tables and slides
Visual layout is where OCR loses information.
What are costs of multi-vector indexes? Select all that apply.
Need for a store that supports MaxSim
Recall on detail is usually higher.
1,000 × 128 × 2 bytes per page is about how much?
Where can ColBERT sit besides first-stage retrieval?
As a re-ranker over a cheaper first stage
Recall rises from 69% to 85%. On 1,000 questions, how many more find the page?
Which reduce multi-vector index size? Select all that apply.
Why can single vectors miss a clause detail?
One vector summarises the whole passage and blurs specifics
Compression into one vector loses detail.
A corpus is clean digital text and a tuned dense model gets 92% recall. Is ColBERT worth it?
Only if measured gains justify the larger index
Which vector databases support multi-vector MaxSim?
A query has 5 tokens; best matches are 0.9, 0.8, 0.7, 0.6, 0.5. MaxSim score?
Discharge summaries are photographed by patients. Which retriever suits them?
Visual retrieval handles photos and layouts.
Uncompressed index 260 GB; compressed 40 GB. Reduction?
Before adopting late interaction, measure… Select all that apply.
Which library makes ColBERT easy to try?
Why does late interaction help exact terms?
Each query token can match the same token in the document
Token-level matching keeps exact terms visible.
What is a patch in ColPali?
A small square region of a page image
Latency grows from 20 ms to 90 ms. Within a 150 ms budget?

semantic.q: In your own words: how does semantic search find an answer that shares no words with the question?
semantic.model: An embedding model turns each chunk and the question into dense vectors, and it was trained so that texts with similar meaning get nearby vectors. Search embeds the question with the same model and returns the chunks with the highest cosine similarity. “can I get my money back?” lands near the refund policy because the meanings are close, even though no words match.

semantic.q: How would you choose an embedding model for a bank’s help centre in English and Hindi?
semantic.model: Shortlist a few multilingual models using MTEB retrieval results, then build a test set of a few hundred real customer questions in both languages with known answers and compare recall@k. Weigh cost, latency, vector size and whether data may leave your environment: a self-hosted model such as bge-m3 may beat a hosted API for a bank.

semantic.q: Semantic search misses queries like “ERR_ORD_1045”. Why, and what do you do?
pts: codes carry little meaning for a dense model
semantic.model: An error code is a rare token with almost no semantic content, so its vector is close to many unrelated texts and the right runbook does not stand out. Keep a BM25 index, which weighs rare terms heavily, and fuse its results with the vector results using reciprocal rank fusion.

bm25.q: Explain the three ingredients of a BM25 score.
bm25.model: Each query term contributes its IDF, which is high when few documents contain it, times a term-frequency factor that grows with occurrences but saturates, controlled by k1. The saturation point is scaled by the document’s length relative to the average, controlled by b, so long documents don’t win just by being long. The document’s score is the sum over query terms.

bm25.q: Why do most production retrieval systems keep BM25 next to dense vectors?
bm25.model: BM25 and dense vectors fail in different places. BM25 nails exact tokens such as error codes, SKUs and names, while dense vectors handle paraphrases and synonyms. Fusing their rankings, for example with reciprocal rank fusion, usually beats either alone, and BM25 is cheap, fast and explainable.

bm25.q: Your BM25 results favour long, repetitive pages. What would you change?
bm25.model: Increase b toward 1 so length normalization penalises long pages more, and check that k1 is not so high that repeated terms keep adding score. Also look at tokenization and index titles as a separate, boosted field, so a focused page with the term in its title ranks above a long page that mentions it many times.

multimodal.q: Explain how CLIP-style models let a text query find a photo.
multimodal.model: A CLIP-style model has an image encoder and a text encoder, trained together on millions of image–caption pairs with a contrastive loss, so matching pairs get nearby vectors in one shared space. At search time the text query is embedded by the text encoder and compared with image vectors by cosine similarity.

multimodal.q: How would you search thousands of scanned KYC forms and slide decks?
pts: OCR or layout parsing into text
multimodal.model: Either extract text with OCR and layout parsing and embed it, or embed the page images directly with a document-image retriever such as ColPali, which keeps tables, stamps and layout. Many systems combine both. Test them on real queries, because scans and charts vary a lot.

multimodal.q: What can go wrong with image embeddings, and how do you guard against it?
pts: fine detail such as small text is lost
multimodal.model: Image embeddings capture overall content but often miss fine detail such as small printed text or exact counts, and quality drops in specialised domains such as medical images. Index descriptions or OCR text alongside the images, keep metadata for filtering, and test cross-modal queries in both directions.

contrastive.q: Explain contrastive fine-tuning to a product manager.
pts: pairs of queries and correct answers
pull matches together, push others apart
contrastive.model: We show the model real questions with the article that answered them, plus similar-looking wrong articles. Training moves each question’s vector closer to its right answer and away from the wrong ones, so the model learns our domain’s distinctions, such as MTF versus mutual funds. We prove it on held-out real queries before switching.

contrastive.q: Why can a very low training loss still mean poor retrieval?
contrastive.model: If the negatives are all easy, far away from the query, the softmax already puts almost all probability on the positive, so the loss is near zero and there is nothing to learn, while a look-alike that is not in the loss still outranks the right answer. Include hard negatives, and judge the model by held-out recall, not by loss.

contrastive.q: What does the temperature do in an InfoNCE loss?
contrastive.model: Similarities are divided by the temperature before the softmax. A low temperature such as 0.05 turns small similarity gaps into large probability gaps, which focuses training on the hardest negatives. A high temperature flattens the distribution, so the loss stays high and the gradient weakly separates matches from non-matches.

dimred.q: Compute the memory for 20 million vectors at 1,024 dimensions in float32, int8 and binary.
dimred.model: float32: 1,024 × 4 bytes = 4,096 bytes × 20 million ≈ 81.9 GB. int8: 1,024 bytes × 20 million ≈ 20.5 GB. Binary: 1,024 bits = 128 bytes × 20 million ≈ 2.56 GB.

dimred.q: Compare Matryoshka truncation and quantization. When would you use each?
pts: quantization uses fewer bits per value
truncation needs a model trained for it
dimred.model: Truncation keeps fewer dimensions and only works well with models trained Matryoshka-style. Quantization keeps every dimension but stores each in fewer bits: int8 is 4× smaller with a small loss, binary 32× smaller with a larger one. They combine, for example 512 dimensions in int8, and either can be followed by rescoring with full vectors.

dimred.q: Binary quantization cut memory 32× but recall fell to 82%. What do you do?
dimred.model: Fetch several times more candidates than you need using the fast binary vectors, for example 40 for a top 10, then rescore those candidates with full-precision vectors kept on disk. Measure recall again: this typically recovers most of the loss while RAM holds only the binary index.

multiling.q: Explain how you would serve English, Hindi and Hinglish users from one English help centre with embedding search.
multiling.model: Embed articles and queries with a multilingual model such as BGE-M3 or multilingual-e5, so a Hindi query lands near the English article with the same meaning. Normalise queries with Unicode NFC and transliterate Roman Hindi to Devanagari, keeping English words as typed. Build a test set labelled by language from real chats and report recall@5 per slice. If a slice is still weak, index translated copies of the articles, and de-duplicate results by article id.

multiling.q: Queries are 50% English, 25% Hindi and 25% Hinglish. Recall@5 is 87%, 74% and 58%. What is overall recall, and which slice would you fix first? Show the working.
multiling.model: Overall = 0.5 × 87 + 0.25 × 74 + 0.25 × 58 = 43.5 + 18.5 + 14.5 = 76.5%. Hinglish is the weakest slice at 58%, so fix it first, usually by transliterating Roman Hindi before embedding; in the playground that lifts it to 72% and overall to 80.0%.

multiling.q: After switching to a multilingual model, Hindi recall is good but Hinglish recall barely moved, and the embedding bill for the new Hindi copies is higher than planned. Diagnose both.
pts: budget on measured Hindi token counts
multiling.model: Hinglish is ASCII, so a check such as isascii() or a script test treats it as English and skips transliteration, and varied spellings like “aayega” and “ayega” scatter in the vector space. Detect Roman Hindi with a word list or language-identification model and transliterate it. The bill is higher because Devanagari splits into more tokens per word than English; a budget based on English chunk sizes undercounts it. Measure token counts on real Hindi chunks before estimating cost.

lateint.q: Explain late interaction and when it is worth the cost.
lateint.model: Late interaction keeps a vector per token (ColBERT) or image patch (ColPali) and scores by summing each query token’s best match. It is worth it when single vectors miss detail or documents are scanned and visual, provided you compress the index or use it as a re-ranker.

lateint.q: 1,000 patch vectors of 128 dims at 2 bytes each, for 10 lakh pages. Index size?
lateint.model: 1,000 × 128 × 2 = 256 KB per page; × 10 lakh pages ≈ 256 GB before compression.

lateint.q: Search over scanned bills misses totals and dates even after OCR. What would you try?
lateint.model: OCR loses the table layout that ties a number to its label. Index the page images with a ColPali-family model, compress the patch vectors, and compare recall on your own questions against the OCR pipeline.

cases.title: The help centre customers say never finds anything
cases.brief: A stockbroker's help centre and in-app assistant search 60,000 article chunks with keyword search only, on Postgres full-text. Satisfaction with search is 41%. All the content is text, the index runs on one 8 GB server, and the product head has a quarter to fix it. Someone has already proposed replacing keyword search with vectors outright.
evidence: Of 1,000 failed searches reviewed by hand, 46% are paraphrases: “money cut twice” should find “Duplicate debit reversal” and finds nothing.
19% contain exact tokens - ERR_ORD_1045, ISINs, scheme codes - which the current keyword index already handles well.
31% of in-app queries are Hinglish or Devanagari (“paisa do baar kat gaya”). The overall recall number looks acceptable because the English slice carries the average.
Eighteen months of search logs with clicks are available, and off-the-shelf embeddings rank near-misses above true matches for broker jargon such as STT, pledge and margin shortfall.
cases.task: Choose the techniques you would apply, put them in order, and say which symptom each one fixes. Then compare with the model answer.

why.semantic: Start here. 46% of failures are the same gap: the customer's words and the article's words mean the same thing and share no tokens, which is precisely what keyword search cannot do and what embeddings are for. It is also the largest single slice, so it is the one fix that moves the 41% visibly.
