why.bm25: Keep it, deliberately. 19% of queries turn on exact tokens that the current index already handles well, and embeddings are weak on IDs, codes and rare names - so the proposal to replace keyword search with vectors would trade one failure class for another. Run both and combine them.
why.multiling: 31% of in-app queries are Hinglish or Devanagari against English content, and an English-only model turns Devanagari into near-meaningless vectors. The overall recall number is hiding this slice, which is the real lesson: report recall per language, and choose a model that handles cross-lingual retrieval, Hindi query to English circular.
why.contrastive: Useful, and you have what it needs: eighteen months of clicks is real training signal, and broker jargon ranking near-misses first is exactly the symptom it fixes. Not first, because fine-tuning means re-embedding the whole corpus, and you want the model and language decisions settled before you pay that once.
why.lateint: Useful later: help articles are short and clean, so a tuned single-vector baseline will likely be enough. Worth measuring as a middle stage if precision on long troubleshooting articles stays poor.
why.multimodal: Not needed: the evidence says all content is text. Multimodal embeddings would add vector size and storage to search a corpus that contains no images.
why.dimred: Not needed on these numbers, and it is worth doing the arithmetic: 60,000 chunks at 1,536 float32 dimensions is about 369 MB on an 8 GB server. There is nothing to compress away, and truncating a model not trained for it would cost recall for no benefit.

firstWhy.bm25: Half right, and an important instinct - keeping it is a deliberate decision, not an oversight. But it is already in place and already working on its 19%; choosing it as the first move means your first sprint changes nothing for the 46% who cannot find anything today.
firstWhy.multiling: This is the most neglected slice and the most interesting finding on the page, since one overall number is hiding a failing language. But a multilingual model is still a semantic model, so you are choosing the embedding step either way - decide that you need meaning-based retrieval, then pick the model that covers Hindi too.
firstWhy.contrastive: You have the clicks, so this is tempting and it will help. But fine-tuning adapts an embedding model you have not adopted yet, and it forces a full re-embed of 60,000 chunks - do it once, after the model choice, not before it.

cases.model: Start with semantic embeddings, because 46% of failed searches are paraphrases with no shared tokens, which keyword search structurally cannot answer and which is the largest slice of the complaint. Keep BM25 rather than replacing it: 19% of queries hinge on error codes, ISINs and scheme codes that embeddings blur, so run both and combine them by rank rather than letting one replace the other. Choose a multilingual, code-mixed model for the embedding step, because 31% of in-app queries are Hinglish or Devanagari against English content and an English-only model would turn those into noise - and start reporting recall per language, since one overall number is what hid this. Then use the eighteen months of clicks to fine-tune with contrastive training for broker jargon, in the same pass as the corpus re-embed so you pay that cost once. All the content is text, so multimodal embeddings have nothing to do; and 60,000 vectors is about 369 MB on an 8 GB server, so there is no case for truncation or quantisation at all.
cases.note: Two of the four fixes here force a full re-embed, so the order is partly about paying that once. Case 2 is a corpus where text retrieval has nothing to work with and the compression question is real, and Case 3 is where fine-tuning comes first - so do not carry “start with semantic” forward as a rule.

semantic: Symptom 1 is 46% of all failures and it has a shape: “money cut twice” and “Duplicate debit reversal” mean the same thing and share not one word. What kind of representation puts those two close together?
You need the match to be about meaning rather than overlap of tokens - which is a different kind of vector from the one a keyword index builds.
Semantic Embeddings. Read the pitfalls too, because one of them explains why you must not throw the keyword index away.
bm25: Symptom 2: 19% of queries contain ERR_ORD_1045, ISINs and scheme codes, and the current search already handles them well. Someone wants to replace that search entirely. What would be lost?

The technique to name here is the one already running - the point is recognising it as a component worth keeping rather than a legacy to remove, because the thing replacing it is weak exactly where this is strong.
Sparse Keyword Search (BM25). Note what it cannot do, and then look at which half of your traffic needs each.
multiling: Symptom 3: 31% of in-app queries are written in Hinglish or Devanagari while every article is in English, and the headline recall number looks fine. What is that number doing, and what does Devanagari become if the model never saw it?
This is about which embedding model you choose rather than whether to use one - and about reporting results in a way that cannot hide a failing slice.
Multilingual and Code-Mixed Embeddings. The pitfall about one overall recall number hiding a failing language is symptom 3 exactly.

drop.multimodal: Multimodal embeddings put text and images in one space. What does the evidence say the corpus is made of?
drop.dimred: Reduced and quantised vectors exist for corpora whose index no longer fits in memory. Do the arithmetic: 60,000 chunks at 1,536 float32 dimensions, on an 8 GB server - what are you saving?

cases.firstHint: Your set is right. Now notice that three of your four choices are really one decision - which embedding model you adopt - and that two of them force you to re-embed all 60,000 chunks. Sequence so you pay that once.

whyFirst.q: Before you check - which is the strongest reason for a step to go first in this case?
options: 31% of in-app queries are in a language the current model cannot represent, and the headline metric is hiding it.
46% of failures are paraphrases that no keyword index can match, which is the largest slice and the reason satisfaction is 41%.
Eighteen months of click logs are already available, so the training signal is sitting there unused.
whyFirst.why: Order by the size of the gap each one closes, when they are all the same kind of change. The language slice is real and must be covered by the model you pick - but picking a multilingual model is still picking an embedding model, so the first decision is that meaning-based retrieval is needed at all. Fine-tuning is last of the three because it adapts a model you have to choose first, and because it makes you re-embed the corpus.

cases.tag: When there is no text to search
cases.title: The archive where text retrieval has nothing to match
cases.brief: A bank's operations team searches an archive of 23 million scanned pages: account statements, cheque images, signed indemnity forms, stamped agreements and annual-report pages full of tables and charts. The current search runs over an OCR text layer. Handlers describe searching for pages they can picture exactly and getting nothing back, and the last attempt to shrink the index made things worse.
evidence: 71% of the corpus is scanned images. On pre-2015 pages the OCR layer is missing or garbled, so the text index has almost nothing to match against.
Handlers search by what a page looks like - “the page with the signature block above the two-column table”, “the chart with the dip in Q3” - which no text index can represent.
On the pages whose OCR is clean, queries turn on exact terms buried in long dense pages, and one vector per page blurs them. A tuned single-vector baseline was never measured.
The multi-vector index is stored uncompressed and the server is out of memory. Binary quantisation was switched on without measuring recall, and results collapsed.
cases.task: Choose the techniques you would apply, put them in order, and say which symptom each one fixes. Then compare with the model answer.

why.multimodal: Start here, because symptoms 1 and 2 are the same wall: 71% of the corpus is pixels, the OCR layer that stands in for it is missing or garbled on older pages, and handlers are describing layout rather than words. Embedding the page image itself is the only thing that gives those queries anything to match - and it removes the dependency on an OCR step that has already failed.
why.lateint: One vector per page is too coarse for a dense scanned page where the answer is one clause or one figure. Late interaction keeps per-token or per-patch vectors so an exact term can light up its own region, and ColPali is built for precisely this material - scanned forms, statements, tables and slides. Measure against a tuned single-vector baseline first, because the evidence says nobody has.
why.dimred: Uncompressed multi-vectors are why the server is out of memory - this is the named pitfall of the technique above, so the two have to be planned together. Compress deliberately: keep the original vectors so you can rescore, oversample when searching binary vectors, and measure recall against exact search rather than reporting the speed-up.
why.semantic: Useful on the clean-OCR portion, where paraphrase queries still need meaning-based matching. Secondary because it depends on text that three quarters of this corpus does not reliably have.
why.bm25: Useful and nearly free where the OCR is good: policy numbers, cheque numbers and claim references are exact tokens, and keyword search is strong on those. It just cannot help on the 71% that has no trustworthy text at all.
why.contrastive: Not needed yet: there is no mention of near-misses outranking true matches, and no click or ticket signal in this evidence. Fine-tuning would also force a re-embed of 23 million pages, which is a heavy bill for a problem nobody has measured.
why.multiling: Not needed on this evidence: no symptom mentions a language. Worth revisiting if regional-language forms turn out to be a slice, but today the failure is that the pages are images, not that they are in Hindi.

firstWhy.lateint: Right about granularity, and it is your second step. But late interaction over the OCR text layer still cannot see a page whose OCR is missing, which is most of the archive - and ColPali, the version that would help, is a multimodal model, so you are choosing that first either way.
firstWhy.dimred: Urgent in the sense that the server is out of memory right now, and the botched binary quantisation needs undoing today. As an ordering choice, though, you would be sizing an index whose contents you are about to change completely - compression is a property of the representation you end up with.
firstWhy.bm25: Cheap, strong on exact tokens, and worth keeping wherever the OCR is clean. But it is a text technique, and the central fact of this case is that 71% of the corpus has no reliable text.

cases.model: Start with multimodal embeddings, because the core problem is not that retrieval is imprecise but that for 71% of the corpus there is nothing to retrieve over: the OCR layer is missing or garbled, and handlers are describing layout and charts rather than words. Embedding the page image directly gives those queries something to match and removes the dependence on a failed OCR step. Then adopt late interaction - ColPali is designed for exactly this material - so a dense scanned page is represented by many vectors rather than one, and an exact clause or figure can light up its own region; measure it against a tuned single-vector baseline, which nobody has done. Plan compression in the same breath, because uncompressed multi-vectors are the documented way to run out of memory: keep the original vectors so rescoring is possible, oversample when searching compressed ones, and report recall against exact search rather than a speed-up - the collapse after binary quantisation was switched on blind is the warning. Keep text retrieval, semantic and BM25, for the portion with clean OCR. Fine-tuning and multilingual models address nothing in this evidence and would each cost a full re-embed of 23 million pages.
cases.note: Case 1's corpus was clean text and compression was arithmetic nobody needed to do; here the compression question is forced by the representation you chose, which is why the two techniques have to be planned as one. Count what the corpus is actually made of before choosing a retrieval technique.

multimodal: Read symptoms 1 and 2 together. 71% of pages are images whose OCR is missing or garbled, and handlers are searching for a signature block above a two-column table, or a chart with a dip. What is the search currently operating on, and what is it missing entirely?
Stop going through a text layer that may not exist. Put the page itself and the query into the same space, so layout and figures are searchable rather than transcribed first.
Multimodal Embeddings. Note the pitfall about fine visual detail such as small text, and the one about storage per item - the second matters for your third step.
lateint: Symptom 3: on pages where the OCR is clean, the query turns on an exact term buried in a long dense page, and one vector for the whole page blurs it. What do you do when a single vector per passage loses too much?
Keep many vectors per page rather than one, and let the query's parts match the page's parts. One named variant of this is built specifically for scanned forms, statements and slides.
Late Interaction and Multi-Vector (ColBERT, ColPali). Read the pitfall about skipping the tuned single-vector baseline - symptom 3 says nobody measured it - and the one about memory.
dimred: Symptom 4: the multi-vector index is uncompressed, the server is out of memory, and someone switched on binary quantisation without measuring and watched results collapse. What is the disciplined version of what they tried?

Smaller vectors, chosen rather than assumed - with the originals kept so a precise rescore is still possible, extra candidates pulled when the vectors are coarse, and recall measured against exact search.

Matryoshka, Quantised and Reduced Embeddings. All three pitfalls are in this symptom: truncating a model not trained for it, binary vectors without oversampling, and conclusions drawn without measurement.

drop.contrastive: Contrastive fine-tuning fixes near-misses outranking true matches, and it needs real signal such as clicks or tickets. Which symptom reports a ranking problem, and where is the training data?
drop.multiling: Multilingual embeddings matter when customers write in one language and the content is in another. Which of these four symptoms mentions a language at all?

cases.firstHint: You have the right three, and they are more coupled than they look: the second one multiplies the number of vectors per page, which is what makes the third one unavoidable. Start with the one that decides whether there is anything to embed at all.

whyFirst.q: Before you check - which is the strongest reason for a step to go first in this case?
options: For most of the corpus there is no reliable text, so no text-based technique has anything to operate on.
The server is out of memory today and a botched quantisation has already collapsed recall, so capacity is the live incident.
One vector per page is too coarse for dense documents, which is the deepest retrieval-quality problem here.
whyFirst.why: Order by what is representable before what is precise. The memory problem is real and the granularity problem is the subtlest finding, but both are properties of a representation - and for 71% of these pages the representation currently does not exist, because the OCR it depends on is missing. Decide what you are embedding first; the other two are then decisions about the thing you chose.

cases.tag: Jargon, and paying for it once
cases.title: The clause search that keeps finding the clause next door
cases.brief: A legal-operations team searches 90 million contract clauses so reviewers can find precedent wording. The content is clean digital text in English. Reviewers say the search is confidently wrong: it returns something adjacent to what they asked for, ranked first. A previous fine-tuning attempt made general queries worse, and the index has outgrown the machine it runs on.
evidence: Off-the-shelf embeddings rank near-misses above true matches: “limitation of liability” returns “limitation period” and “indemnity cap” ahead of the actual clause. Six years of review tickets give 240,000 labelled query-clause pairs.
An earlier attempt fine-tuned on 900 examples from one practice area. General queries got measurably worse and the model was rolled back.
The corpus is 90 million clauses. At 1,024 float32 dimensions the vectors need about 345 GB, and the index no longer fits in the 128 GB machine.
Queries routinely carry exact defined terms and section references - “Section 7.2(b)”, “Permitted Transferee” - which the embeddings blur into near neighbours.
cases.task: Choose the techniques you would apply, put them in order, and say which symptom each one fixes. Then compare with the model answer.

why.contrastive: Start here, and the reason is as much economic as technical. Near-misses outranking true matches on specialised jargon is the symptom contrastive training exists for, and 240,000 labelled pairs from six years of tickets is the signal it needs. The earlier failure is instructive rather than disqualifying: 900 examples from one practice area is overfitting to a small dataset, which is a named pitfall, and the fix is breadth and held-out evaluation, not abandonment. Watch for false negatives in the pairs - genuinely relevant clauses labelled as non-matches will teach the model the wrong thing.
why.dimred: 345 GB of float32 vectors on a 128 GB machine is a hard constraint, and Matryoshka truncation or quantisation is how it is met. It belongs immediately after the model decision for one practical reason: a fine-tuned model means re-embedding all 90 million clauses, and so does a change of dimensionality - do them in one pass or pay for the largest job in this project twice.
why.bm25: “Section 7.2(b)” and “Permitted Transferee” are exact tokens, and embeddings are weak on exactly that - defined terms are near-identical in meaning to their neighbours and distinguished only by the literal string. Keyword search handles them, costs little, and is independent of the re-embed, so it can ship in parallel.
why.semantic: Useful as the foundation the first step builds on - the fine-tuned model is still a semantic embedding model, and reviewers' paraphrases need meaning-based matching. It is not a separate decision so much as the starting point.
why.lateint: Useful as a middle stage: clauses are long and exact terms matter, which is the case late interaction is made for. Secondary because the per-clause multi-vectors would worsen the memory problem you are already solving, so measure the tuned single-vector baseline first.
why.multimodal: Not needed: the evidence says the content is clean digital text. Using a page-image model on clean text is a documented waste - text retrieval is cheaper and better here.
why.multiling: Not needed: the corpus and the queries are both English. No symptom describes a language slice at all.

firstWhy.dimred: The constraint is real and immediate - 345 GB does not go into 128 GB, and nothing ships until it does. But truncating or quantising commits you to a vector size for a model you are about to replace, and re-embedding 90 million clauses is the biggest single cost in this project. Choose the model, then choose its size, in one pass.
firstWhy.bm25: Cheapest fix on the page, independent of everything else, and you should start it in parallel rather than queue it. As the first move, though, it addresses the 19th-percentile problem: defined terms are a slice, while “confidently returns the clause next door” is the complaint reviewers actually make.
firstWhy.semantic: True as a foundation, but it is what you already have - off-the-shelf semantic embeddings are what is ranking “limitation period” first. The decision in front of you is whether to adapt them, not whether to adopt them.

cases.model: Start with contrastive fine-tuning, because the complaint - near-misses ranked above true matches on legal jargon - is precisely what it fixes, and 240,000 labelled pairs from six years of review tickets is real signal. Treat the previous failure as a lesson in method: 900 examples from one practice area is textbook overfitting to a small dataset, so train across practice areas, hold out a general-query evaluation set, and audit the pairs for false negatives, since relevant clauses marked as non-matches teach the model the opposite of what you want. Pair that immediately with dimensionality reduction - 345 GB of float32 does not fit a 128 GB machine - using Matryoshka truncation or quantisation chosen by measured recall, and do it in the same pass as the fine-tune, because both force a full re-embed of 90 million clauses and that is the most expensive job here. Separately and in parallel, add BM25 for defined terms and section references, which embeddings blur and keyword search nails. Late interaction is worth measuring afterwards against the tuned single-vector baseline, bearing in mind it multiplies the memory you have just economised. The content is clean English digital text, so multimodal and multilingual models have nothing to contribute.
cases.note: The first move here is not the biggest number or the hardest constraint - it is the decision the expensive step depends on, because fine-tuning and resizing both force a re-embed and should happen together. Across the three cases the first move went to whatever the corpus itself demanded: meaning in Case 1, pixels in Case 2, the domain's own vocabulary here.

contrastive: Read symptoms 1 and 2 together. The search confidently returns “limitation period” for “limitation of liability”, there are 240,000 labelled query-clause pairs from six years of tickets, and an earlier attempt using 900 examples from one practice area made general queries worse. What technique is all of that about - including the failure?

The off-the-shelf model has not learned this domain's distinctions. There is a way to teach it using pairs you already have, and symptom 2 is one of its named failure modes rather than evidence against it.
Contrastive Embeddings. Read all three pitfalls: false negatives in the pairs, overfitting to a small dataset - which is symptom 2 exactly - and the full re-embed it forces.
dimred: Symptom 3: 90 million clauses, about 345 GB of float32 vectors, and a 128 GB machine. What makes vectors smaller without throwing away recall - and what has to be measured rather than assumed?
Shorter vectors, or coarser ones, chosen deliberately. Note which models can be truncated safely and which cannot, and what you must keep if you want to rescore.
Matryoshka, Quantised and Reduced Embeddings. Read the first pitfall about truncating a model not trained for it - it links straight back to your model choice.
bm25: Symptom 4: “Section 7.2(b)” and “Permitted Transferee”. Those are not paraphrases - they are literal strings whose meaning is almost identical to their neighbours. What kind of search is strongest on exact tokens?
The sparse half of a hybrid setup, matching the words as written rather than what they mean. It is also the one fix here that needs no re-embedding at all.
Sparse Keyword Search (BM25). Note where it is strong and where it is useless, then look at which slice of these queries needs which.

drop.multimodal: Multimodal embeddings put images and text in one space. What does the brief say this corpus is made of - and what does the technique's own pitfall say about using it on clean digital text?
drop.multiling: Multilingual and code-mixed embeddings serve customers writing in one language against content in another. What language are these contracts and these queries in?

cases.firstHint: Your set is right and one of your choices is load-bearing for another. Two of these three force you to re-embed 90 million clauses - work out which decision has to be made before that job runs, because you only want to run it once.

whyFirst.q: Before you check - which is the strongest reason for a step to go first in this case?
options: 345 GB of vectors does not fit a 128 GB machine, so nothing can ship until the index is made to fit.
The model has to be chosen before the vectors are sized, because both changes force the same full re-embed of 90 million clauses.
Defined terms and section references are the cheapest symptom to fix and need no re-embedding at all.
whyFirst.why: Order by what the expensive step depends on. The memory constraint is hard and the keyword fix is cheap - and the keyword work should run in parallel, since it touches none of this. But fine-tuning and resizing are two decisions about the same artefact, and re-embedding 90 million clauses is the largest job in the project. Decide the model, then its dimensionality, then embed once.

quiz: Users search “money deducted twice”. The right article is titled “Duplicate debit reversal”. Keyword search finds nothing. What helps most?
The query and title share no words but mean the same thing. Dense embeddings match meaning.
Queries like “ERR_ORD_1045” return generic results from vector search. What's the fix?
Add BM25 and fuse it with vector search
Exact rare tokens are BM25's strength. Hybrid search keeps both.
Mid-chat, “what about the other one?” retrieves unrelated documents. What's the fix?
LLM query rewriting using the chat history
The query alone has no content to search on. Rewrite it into a standalone query first.
Customers upload photos of damaged parts to find the right spare. Which technique?
Images and product text need to share one vector space.
Your embeddings treat “MTF” and “MF” as nearly identical. What's the best long-term fix?
Training on real query–article pairs with look-alike wrong answers teaches the model your domain's distinctions.
20 million vectors × 1,536 float32 dimensions. How much memory do the raw vectors need?
You switch to a new embedding model. What must you do?
Vectors from different models live in different spaces and can't be compared.
In BM25, why does “the” add almost nothing to a document's score?
Its IDF is tiny because it appears in almost every document
IDF rewards rare terms; a word in every document carries no signal.
A cross-encoder is more accurate than a bi-encoder. Why not use it for all retrieval?
It must read every query–document pair together, which is too slow over millions
Document vectors can't be precomputed for a cross-encoder, so it's used to re-rank a short list.
Binary quantization cut memory 32×, but recall dropped. What's the standard remedy?
Oversample candidates and re-rank with full-precision vectors
Retrieve more cheap candidates, then rescore them precisely: most recall comes back at a fraction of the memory.

semantic.t: Compute the cosine similarity of a = [1, 2, 2] and b = [2, 1, 2].
semantic.a: a · b = 2 + 2 + 4 = 8. ‖a‖ = ‖b‖ = 3. Cosine = 8 ÷ 9 ≈ 0.889: very similar direction.
iv: What's the difference between a bi-encoder and a cross-encoder?

A bi-encoder embeds query and document separately, so document vectors are precomputed and search is fast. A cross-encoder reads them together for more accurate relevance but can't precompute, so it's used to re-rank a short list.
How do you choose a chunk size?
Big enough to hold a complete idea, small enough to be specific: often 200–800 tokens with some overlap, split on headings or paragraphs. Tune it by measuring recall@k on real questions.
mis: Embedding queries and documents with different models
Use the same model, including any required query/document prefixes
Fixed-size chunks that cut sentences and tables
Chunk on structure: headings, paragraphs, table boundaries

bm25.t: In 1,000 documents, “error” appears in 400 and “E1045” in 2. Using IDF ≈ ln(N ÷ df), how many times more does “E1045” weigh than “error”?
bm25.a: ln(1000 ÷ 400) ≈ 0.92 and ln(1000 ÷ 2) ≈ 6.21, so “E1045” weighs about 6.8× more. (BM25's exact IDF formula differs slightly; the idea is the same.)
iv: Why keep BM25 when you have embeddings?
Embeddings blur exact tokens like error codes, SKUs, names and rare jargon, which BM25 matches precisely. Hybrid search combines both and usually beats either alone.
What do k1 and b control in BM25?
k1 sets term-frequency saturation (how much repeats keep adding); b sets document-length normalization (0 none, 1 full). Typical values are k1 ≈ 1.2–2.0 and b ≈ 0.75.
mis: Different tokenization at index and query time
Use the same analyzer for both
BM25 alone for natural-language questions
Pair it with dense retrieval in a hybrid

multimodal.t: With a CLIP model, a text query scores 0.31, 0.12 and 0.29 against three images. Image 1 is the right match. Why are the scores so low, and what matters?
multimodal.a: Text–image similarities in CLIP-style models are usually low in absolute terms. What matters is the ranking: image 1 comes first. Tune any threshold per model on your own data.
iv: How does CLIP put text and images in one space?
It trains an image encoder and a text encoder together with a contrastive loss on image–caption pairs, pulling matching pairs together and pushing mismatched ones apart.
How would you search scanned PDFs full of charts and tables?
Either OCR and layout parsing into text chunks, or embed page images directly with a document-image model such as ColPali, which keeps the visual layout. Many systems combine both.
mis: Comparing similarity scores across models
Tune thresholds per model on your data
Dropping the link to the original asset
Store the asset URL and extracted text as metadata

contrastive.t: A training batch holds 32 (query, positive) pairs. With in-batch negatives, how many negatives does each query see?
contrastive.a: 31: every other positive in the batch acts as a negative, which is why larger batches often train better.
iv: What are hard negatives, and why do they matter?
Passages that look relevant but are wrong, such as a mutual-fund article for an MTF query. Easy negatives teach little; hard negatives force the model to learn your domain's fine distinctions.
How do you know fine-tuning helped?
Hold out a labelled set of real queries and compare recall@k and MRR against the base model, and check that general queries didn't get worse.
mis: Mining “negatives” that are actually relevant
Filter false negatives, for example with a cross-encoder
Evaluating on the training pairs
Use a held-out set of real queries

dimred.t: 10 million vectors at 1,024 float32 dimensions. How much memory with int8 quantization, in GB?
iv: What is Matryoshka representation learning?
Training an embedding model so the first dimensions carry the most information, like nested dolls. You can truncate vectors (say 1,536 → 256) and keep most of the quality without retraining.
Scalar or binary quantization?

Scalar (int8) stores each value in 8 bits: 4× smaller with a small recall loss. Binary stores 1 bit per dimension: 32× smaller but a larger loss, usually recovered by oversampling and re-ranking with full vectors.
mis: Truncating vectors from a model not trained for it
Only truncate Matryoshka-trained models
Judging clusters from a 2-D plot
Measure retrieval metrics in the full space

multiling.t: Kosh Bank indexes 2,40,000 English chunks of 300 tokens each and adds a Hindi translation of every chunk. Each Hindi chunk takes 1.6 times as many tokens as its English original. How many extra tokens, in millions, does embedding the Hindi copies add?
multiling.a: Hindi chunk: 300 × 1.6 = 480 tokens. 2,40,000 × 480 = 11,52,00,000 tokens = 115.2 million, on top of the 72 million for the English chunks.
iv: How would you make an English help centre searchable in Hindi and Hinglish?

Use a multilingual embedding model such as BGE-M3 or multilingual-e5 so Hindi queries land near English articles. Normalise queries with Unicode NFC and transliterate Roman Hindi to Devanagari. Build a test set labelled by language from real chat logs, report recall@5 per slice, and add translated copies of the articles only where a slice still falls short.
Why is a single overall recall figure dangerous for multilingual search?

It is a weighted average, so a large English slice can hide a failing smaller one. With 50% English at 88%, 25% Hindi at 8% and 25% Hinglish at 35%, overall is 54.8%, which looks mediocre rather than broken, yet Hindi users are almost never served. Always report each language separately.
mis: Embedding Hindi with an English-only model
Use a multilingual model and check it on a Hindi slice
Treating Hinglish as English because it is ASCII
Detect Roman Hindi and transliterate it, or test that the model handles it as typed

lateint.t: A page produces 1,000 patch vectors of 128 dimensions stored as 2-byte numbers. How many KB does one page need?
lateint.a: 1,000 × 128 × 2 bytes = 2,56,000 bytes, about 256 KB (roughly 250 KiB). Ten lakh pages need about 256 GB before compression.
iv: What is late interaction?

Queries and documents are encoded into one vector per token, and the score sums each query token’s best match in the document (MaxSim). It keeps detail that a single vector loses, at the cost of a bigger index.
When would you use ColPali?
When documents are scanned or visual, such as forms, bills, tables and slides, so OCR and layout parsing lose information. It searches page images directly.
mis: Storing uncompressed token vectors
Pool, compress or binarise them
Replacing a tuned baseline without measuring
Compare recall and cost on your own questions

gloss: embedding
A list of numbers representing text or an image so that similar meanings get nearby vectors.
cosine similarity
The cosine of the angle between two vectors: 1 means same direction, 0 unrelated.
chunk
A passage a document is split into before embedding.
bi-encoder
A model that embeds query and document separately; fast because document vectors are precomputed.
cross-encoder
A model that reads query and document together to score relevance; accurate but slow.
IDF
Inverse document frequency: rarer terms get more weight in keyword ranking.
BM25
A keyword ranking function using term frequency, IDF and document length.
HyDE
Hypothetical Document Embeddings: embed an LLM-written sample answer instead of the question.
CLIP
A model trained on image–caption pairs so text and images share one vector space.
hard negative
A wrong result that looks very like the right one; valuable for training.
Matryoshka
Embeddings trained so the first dimensions hold the most information, allowing truncation.
quantization
Storing numbers in fewer bits, such as float32 → int8 or 1 bit, to save memory.
recall@k
Share of relevant items that appear in the top k results.
MRR
Mean reciprocal rank: the average of 1 ÷ rank of the first relevant result.
transliteration
Rewriting text from one script to another without translating it, such as “paisa” to “पैसा”.
cross-lingual retrieval
Search where the query and the document are in different languages, such as a Hindi question finding an English article.
tokenizer fertility
The average number of tokens a tokenizer produces per word; it is usually higher for Devanagari than for English.
language slice
The part of a test set in one language, evaluated and reported on its own.
late interaction
Retrieval that keeps one vector per token and compares query and document tokens at search time.
MaxSim
The late-interaction score: for each query token take its highest similarity to any document token, then sum.
ColPali
A late-interaction model that embeds patches of page images, so documents can be searched without OCR.

multiling.name: Contrastive Embeddings
multiling.note: When an off-the-shelf multilingual model still misses Hinglish phrasing, contrastive fine-tuning on real Hinglish query–article pairs teaches it your customers' spellings.

multiling.note: Hinglish and regional-language personas test the multilingual behaviour real users bring.
